title: How did currencies get their names? | MONEY WORD ORIGINS

entries.note: From Latin [[from:Moneta]], an epithet of [[see:Juno]], at whose temple coins were minted; related to [[same-root:admonish]], [[same-root:mental]], [[same-root:memory]], [[same-root:amnesia]] and [[same-root:mantis]].
Epithet of [[see:Juno]], probably meaning to advise or admonish; her temple was where money was coined, giving [[gave:money]] and [[gave:mint]].
Roman goddess called [[see:Moneta]], whose temple on the Capitoline Hill was where money was coined and precious metals stored.
Related to [[same-root:money]] through [[see:Moneta]], which probably meant to advise or admonish.
One of the thinking words related to [[same-root:money]].
One of the thinking words related to [[same-root:money]].
One of the thinking words related to [[same-root:money]].
Named as related to [[same-root:money]] and the words for thinking.
Also from [[from:Moneta]]; its Old English predecessor also meant coin or money, because the word [[see:coin]] didn't exist yet.
From Latin [[from:cuneus]], corner; in 14th-century English it meant wedge, then a stamped piece of money, after the wedge-like dies used to stamp metal.
An anglicization of [[from:Taler]], short for [[from:Joachimsthaler]], which came via Low German before the US existed; the American dollar later followed the [[see:Spanish dollar]].
Bohemian valley whose silver mines produced coins called [[gave:Joachimsthaler]], the ultimate source of [[gave:dollar]].
Silver coins from the mines of [[from:Joachimsthal]]; the first part was dropped for convenience, leaving [[gave:Taler]].
Short for [[from:Joachimsthaler]] and anglicized as [[gave:dollar]]; still used in Rob's Berlin [[see:Kiez]] for tokens given to elderly people.
German word for a Berlin neighbourhood, where Rob's local scheme gives tokens called [[see:Taler]].
Also called the piece of eight or [[see:peso]]; first minted in 1497, trusted for its consistent silver content and divisible into eight bits. The American dollar adopted the coin idea.
No one knows its origin; theories include PS for [[see:peso]], the [[see:Pillars of Hercules]], a serpent on a cross on [[see:Taler]] coins, and [[see:Ayn Rand]]'s squashed U.
Originally a pound weight of silver worth 240 pence, from [[from:libra pondo]]; called pound [[see:sterling]] to distinguish it from other pounds.
The £ is an L for [[from:libra pondo]]; Americans also use the name for #, now often called a [[see:hash]] or [[see:hashtag]].
Libra is Latin for a weight, also the star sign of the scales; this explains why the [[see:pound sign]] is an L.
Probably a little star, from a Norman coin with a star on it; a less likely theory points to coins with birds on them ([[from?:starling]]s), but the spelling argues against it.
The bird behind a less likely theory for [[see:sterling]], which would then be spelled with -star-.
Presumably follows the same logic as [[see:sterling]], since the pound related directly to a weight of silver.
Literally weight, as in [[from:peso de oro]] and [[from:peso de plata]]; also a name for the [[see:Spanish dollar]] and possibly the source of the [[see:dollar sign]].
One of the full forms behind the currency name [[see:peso]].
One of the full forms behind the currency name [[see:peso]].
Merchant who helped finance the American Revolution from Spanish New Orleans and supposedly merged PS into the [[see:dollar sign]] in ledgers from around 1778.
Financier who adopted the merged PS of [[see:Oliver Pollock]] and officially began using the [[see:dollar sign]] in US correspondence.
Its many shapes, and how close they stay to the Latin et, make the PS theory of the [[see:dollar sign]] believable to Jess.
The Greeks' name for the entrance to the Strait of Gibraltar and a symbol of Spain; shown wrapped in scrolls on Spanish coins, perhaps inspiring the [[see?:dollar sign]].
In her Atlas Shrugged, a character says the two lines of the [[see:dollar sign]] are a squashed U for US; the hosts call it chronologically impossible.
A Greek epsilon with an extra line, officially said to represent stability.
Created only in 2010 from public suggestions; it combines Devanagari ra with a Latin R, and its lines are said to represent the Indian flag and equality.
Chosen in 1995 over [[see:ECU]], [[see:florin]] and [[see:ducat]]; credited to the Esperantist [[see:Germain Pirlot]], though Italian federalists suggested it in the 1960s; it has no nickname.
The original name proposed for the [[see:euro]], an acronym for European currency union, dropped because of the old French coin the [[see:écu (French)]].
Old French coin whose name clashed with the proposed [[see:ECU]].
Britain's suggestion for the [[see:euro]], since many European cultures have had one; in pre-decimal Britain it was worth two [[see:shilling]]s.
Another suggested name for the [[see:euro]].
Swedish and Norwegian currency, one of the many European currencies meaning [[see:crown]].
British coin worth five [[see:shilling]]s and a suggested name for the [[see:euro]]; coins are named crown because they often show someone wearing one.
Belgian Esperantist often credited with the idea of naming the currency the [[see:euro]].
How the French described the name [[see:euro]].
The German name for their currency under Germany's proposal to use [[see:euro]] as a prefix rather than a noun.
The French currency under Germany's proposal to use [[see:euro]] as a prefix.
The Italian currency under Germany's proposal to use [[see:euro]] as a prefix.
The casual word Rob uses for money, unlike the [[see:euro]], which has no nickname.
Germans' nickname for the [[see:euro]] for a time, from [[from:teuer]], expensive; Jess says it has too many syllables.
American slang for money; Rob feels clever using it with his international friends.
One of the many American slang words for money.
One of the many American slang words for money.
American slang for money, also used for the US [[see:dollar]].

A slang term for money that Rob finds quite cute.
Money collected by an entertainer after a performance; Rob really likes the term.
Coined in the US in the 1800s, apparently just an arbitrary, funny-sounding word for money.
From the Romani [[from:wongar]], meaning money or coal, which says something about the historical value of coal.
A slang term for money from Rob's list.
A slang word for money from Rob's list.
An American coinage for money, from Yiddish [[from:af n tish]], money on the table, like the German [[see:auf dem Tisch]].
German phrase that Germans would recognise in the Yiddish source of [[see:oftish]].
First minted in the late 8th century as silver coins worth 1/240 of a Saxon pound; perhaps from [[from?:Pfand]], making it related to [[same-root?:pawn]].
German counterpart of [[same-root:penny]], one of many Germanic forms ending in -ing.
The deposit on returnable cans and bottles; possibly the source of [[gave?:penny]] and related to [[same-root:pawn]].
Related to [[same-root:Pfand]], as discussed in an earlier episode, so a [[see:penny]] may be a pawning.
The base-12 counting behind the 240 pence in a pre-decimal [[see:pound]].
The smallest pre-decimal British denomination, two to a [[see:ha'penny]]; in Middle English sometimes called a [[see:quarter]].
Pre-decimal halfpenny, worth two [[see:farthing]]s; two made a [[see:penny]].
Twelve pence, twenty to the pound; perhaps from the same root as [[same-root?:scale]], [[same-root?:shale]] and [[same-root?:shell]], words meaning fragmented or cut up.
Pre-decimal coin worth three pennies; two made a [[see:sixpence]].
Pre-decimal coin; two made a [[see:shilling]].
Worth two [[see:crown]]s; two made a [[see:pound note]].
Worth 20 shillings, two [[see:ten shilling note]]s or ten [[see:florin]]s.
Pre-decimal coin; two made a [[see:crown]].
Perhaps shares a root meaning fragmented or cut up with [[same-root?:shilling]].
Perhaps shares a root meaning fragmented or cut up with [[same-root?:shilling]].
Perhaps shares a root meaning fragmented or cut up with [[same-root?:shilling]].
The plural of [[same-root:penny]] Britain prefers over pennies, even saying one pence; it rhymes with [[see:cent]].
From Latin [[from:centum]], hundred; began in 1793 with the [[see:chain cent]], gaining its hundredth sense through [[see:percent]]; called a penny from about 1889.
The first [[see:cent]], a copper coin that no one liked or used.
Means per hundred, the notion that gave [[see:cent]] its sense of a hundredth.
A rarely used counterpart of [[see:percent]], written like the percent sign with an extra tiny zero.
Just Hebrew for weight, like the [[see:peso]].
Means to cut; originally a denomination of the [[see:grivna]].
Older currency of which the [[see:ruble]] was a denomination; it sounds very like the Ukrainian [[see:hryvnia]].
Ukraine's currency, meaning neck because coins with holes could be worn on a string around the neck, a practice going back to 11th-century Kievan Rus'.
Old Spanish currency mentioned among coins with holes; its name means little weight.
Early standardized Greek silver coin, from [[from:obelos]], spit or nail, related to [[same-root:obelisk]]; originally a metal rod, six making a [[see:drachma]].
Greek coin worth six [[see:obol]]s, meaning a handful; related to the [[same-root:dirham]] and the source of [[gave:dram]].
Related to [[same-root:obol]].
Moroccan currency related to the [[same-root:drachma]].
A small serving of whisky, also Armenia's currency; both come from the Greek [[from:drachma]], an origin you'd never guess in the Scottish Highlands.
Japan's currency, meaning round coin like the [[see:won]] and [[see:yuan]]; a Portuguese rendering turned the original W sound of the Japanese word into a Y.
Currency of both Koreas, meaning round coin like the [[see:yen]] and [[see:yuan]].
Chinese currency, meaning round coin like the [[see:yen]] and [[see:won]].
Chinese currency name, ren being Mandarin for people.
South Africa's currency, taken from the end of [[from:Witwatersrand]], a gold-mining region.
Gold-mining region with an apparently Afrikaans name, whose ending gave the [[gave:rand]].
Bulgaria's former currency, now replaced by the euro, meaning lion.
Widely considered the first minted coins, from around the 7th century BCE, stamped with lions and made of [[see:electrum]].
Romanian currency, also meaning lion, like the [[see:lev]].
Sierra Leone's currency, ultimately meaning lion, from the country's name [[from:Sierra Leone]].
Country whose name means Lion Mountains, which explains its currency, the [[gave:leone]].
A naturally occurring gold-silver alloy named for its colour after amber, Greek [[from:elektron]], as covered in an earlier episode.
Also named after amber, [[from:elektron]], because rubbing amber was observed to generate sparks.
From Greek [[from:nomisma]]; Rob learned it from a coin-collecting YouTube channel, and Jess knew the editor of a numismatics magazine.
Often mistaken for a president because he appears on money, a mistake Rob once made in a newsletter; also known for his attempt at alphabet reform.
Literally something in circulation, like a river's [[same-root:current]]; a word with currency is current in usage.
A river's current and current meaning now are the same word as [[same-root:currency]]: something that flows.
From Italian for bench, where moneylenders sat; Jess thought it unrelated to riverbank, but it's the same word, as is [[same-root:bench]].
Fiat currency is money sanctioned by, say, a central bank; from Latin for let it be done, related to [[same-root:facere]].
Latin for to make or to do, related to [[same-root:fiat]] and discussed before; it gives French [[gave:faire]] and Italian [[gave:fare (Italian)]].
French verb that comes from [[from:facere]].
Italian verb that comes from [[from:facere]].
Means a broken bench, probably figuratively, though some say a defaulter's bench was publicly smashed.
Etymologically the same word as [[same-root:bank]].
Selling a smaller cut of something, related to [[same-root:tally]] and [[same-root:tailor]]; contrasted with [[see:wholesale]].
A notched stick recording debts; burning old ones caused the 1834 fire at the [[see:Palace of Westminster]]; means to cut, and is cognate with [[same-root:Zahl]].
Destroyed in 1834 by a fire that got out of control while disused [[see:tally]] sticks were being burned.
Given to English by French; without it, Rob conjectures, we'd probably say [[see:tally]].
German word for number, directly related to [[same-root:tally]].
Related to [[same-root:tally]] and [[same-root:retail]] through the sense of cutting.
Selling the whole, in contrast to [[see:retail]], which sells a smaller cut.
From Latin for end, like [[same-root:finite]]; originally a payment that settled a debt, from finalizing accounts.
Shares the Latin root for end with [[same-root:finance]].
A death pledge, referring not to anyone dying but to the deal dying once payment is made or missed; probably discussed before.
Germany's currency before the euro, as the Deutsche Mark and [[see:Reichsmark]]; related to English [[same-root:mark]], because the first marks were cut from stamped ingots.
An earlier German currency, one of the many [[see:Mark (currency)]] currencies over the centuries.
Directly related to the German currency [[same-root:Mark (currency)]], whose first coins were cut from marked ingots.
A weight, then a coin; a biblical parable about investing your talents gave us talented, as covered in the Bible episode.
Every sense comes from chess, via the checked board used for accounting; discussed several times before.
From the Sanskrit [[from:rupya]], a shaped thing.
From German [[from:Kupfernickel]], copper goblin, an ore yielding no copper; became the US five-cent coin after [[see:Joseph Wharton]] lobbied for nickel coins.
Industrialist who owned nickel mines in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, and lobbied hard to make the [[see:nickel]] a coin.
A tiny US silver coin before the [[see:nickel]], first struck in 1792, supposedly with silver donated by [[see:George Washington]].
Supposedly donated the silver for the first [[see:half dime]].
Means tenth, from Old French [[from:disme]] and medieval Latin [[from:decima pars]]; first spelled disme to rhyme with team; related to [[same-root:tithe]] and [[same-root:decimal]].
A tenth owed to the church, ultimately from the same root as [[same-root:dime]].
Ultimately from the same root as [[same-root:dime]].
Used for a coin since Middle English, when a [[see:farthing]] was sometimes called one; the Roman [[see:quadrans]] was a quarter of an as.
Roman coin worth a quarter of an as, an early parallel to the [[see:quarter]].
Name for the copper-nickel clad quarter, which replaced the silver one in 1965 as silver prices rose under [[see:Lyndon B. Johnson]].
The clad quarter came under his presidency and reforms, hence [[see:Johnson sandwich]]; Jess says LBJ would have found the joke hilarious.
A banknote is essentially a promise to pay the bearer, as British notes state, rather than the money itself.
A string of symbols, such as the [[see:dollar sign]] and the # [[see:pound sign]], printed on Rob's T-shirt; explained in an earlier episode.
Another name for the # symbol, which Americans call a [[see:pound sign]] and many now call a [[see:hashtag]].
Now a common name for the # symbol, though Rob insists it's only a hashtag when followed by a word, a tag with a [[see:hash]].
The British name for the game whose grid looks like the # symbol; Americans call it [[equivalent:tic-tac-toe]].
The American name for [[equivalent:noughts and crosses]].
